common_name: Superbells Pomegranate Punch Calibrachoa (Deep Red-Pink Trailing Million Bells)

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring as soon as last hard freeze danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring bloom. Pomegranate Punch is part of the Punch subseries of Superbells bred for extra-vigorous, more sun- and heat-tolerant trailing growth than standard Superbells.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.0), fertile potting mix or garden soil, and feed regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer since calibrachoa is a heavy feeder prone to iron deficiency chlorosis in alkaline soil. Pomegranate Punch is part of the Punch subseries of Proven Winners' Superbells calibrachoa, bred for a deeper, richer red-pink flower color and more vigorous, heat-tolerant trailing growth than standard Superbells selections, cascading in hundreds of small, petunia-like blooms over hanging baskets and container edges. Like other calibrachoa, it is self-cleaning and needs no deadheading, blooming continuously from spring through the point where summer heat and humidity trigger decline in zone 9, typically resuming with fall's cooler temperatures. Its vegetatively propagated uniformity and heavier bloom under stress make it a reliable performer in intense summer sun where some other calibrachoa selections thin out.
sources: Proven Winners — Superbells Punch series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Calibrachoa for Florida Container Gardens

common_name: SunPatiens Compact Orange Impatiens (Sun-Tolerant Season-Long Bedding Impatiens)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; unlike traditional impatiens, SunPatiens tolerates full sun and heat without wilting and is also resistant to downy mildew, the disease that has devastated standard impatiens plantings.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil, and feed regularly through the season to sustain the vigorous growth and nonstop bloom this series is bred for. SunPatiens Compact Orange is a vegetatively propagated, downy-mildew-resistant impatiens hybrid bred to tolerate full sun and heat that would scorch or collapse traditional Impatiens walleriana, holding a dense, well-branched, self-cleaning mound covered in bright orange flowers from spring through frost. The Compact series stays more tidy and controlled than the larger Vigorous SunPatiens line, making it well suited to smaller beds, borders, and container plantings where a large spreading mound would be too much. Consistent moisture is important during establishment and through the hottest stretch of summer, though established plantings tolerate brief dry spells better than traditional impatiens.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Diamond Mound Euphorbia (Compact Mounding Baby's Breath Euphorbia)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into full sun in well-drained soil; Diamond Mound holds a tighter, more rounded habit than the looser, airier Diamond Frost, making it useful as a filler in beds and containers without sprawling.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid overwatering, since this euphorbia is more drought-tolerant than most bedding annuals and dislikes wet, soggy roots. Diamond Mound produces a dense cloud of tiny white flowers over fine-textured foliage almost continuously from spring through frost, giving beds and containers a soft, airy filler texture similar to baby's breath but on a heat-tolerant, low-maintenance annual. Its tighter, more compact mounding habit than the trailing Diamond Frost selection makes it useful as a well-behaved filler that does not spill over neighboring plants, while still needing no deadheading to keep flowering. Established plants tolerate heat and short dry spells well, and light, regular feeding keeps the fine bloom display dense through the growing season; the milky sap can irritate skin, so gloves are recommended when handling or pruning it.
sources: Proven Winners — Diamond euphorbia series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

common_name: Titan Vinca (Large-Flowered Heat-Tolerant Seed Vinca Series)

planting.note: Transplant into warm soil a week or two after the last frost once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Titan thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer once established.

directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid overhead irrigation late in the day since vinca performs best with good air movement around the crown to limit disease. Titan is a large-flowered seed-propagated vinca series bred for exceptionally big, saucer-shaped blooms up to two and a half inches across on compact, mounded plants, providing a bolder floral impact than smaller-flowered vinca types while retaining the class's signature heat and drought tolerance. Once established it blooms continuously from late spring through the first frost with almost no deadheading required, tolerating the intense heat, humidity, and dry spells that wilt many other summer bedding annuals. Its toughness and low maintenance needs have made vinca of all flower sizes a standard choice for hot, sunny beds and highway medians across the Deep South.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Titan vinca series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials
